# Root Cause and CAPA

The step between "we found a bad part" and "we fixed the reason." It is slow,
expert work, and the reason it is slow is that the evidence sits in four systems
that nobody looks at together.

**Two rules govern everything below, and they are the whole character of the
skill:**

**Compute, do not eyeball.** Control limits, run rules and group comparisons are
calculated in code and the skill interprets the computed result. A claim that a
process "was drifting," asserted from looking at a data file, is the first thing
a quality manager will test and the fastest way to lose the room.

**Rank, do not conclude.** The output is candidate causal chains with supporting
*and contradicting* evidence. A confident wrong root cause is worse than a
ranked list, because it closes the investigation and the fix fails.

**Quick start**

```
→ Assemble the evidence window; VERIFY time alignment first
→ Misaligned? Refuse to correlate. Say which conclusions still survive
→ Run the computed checks: SPC drift, clustering, maintenance correlation, recurrence
→ Build candidate chains, each link carrying its own evidence for and against
→ Rank by evidential strength; name what would confirm and what would kill each
→ Draft the 8D: D1-D5 and D7 populated, D6 and D8 left as placeholders
→ Material implicated? Raise the supplier-caused flag for Chain 5
→ Customer pack: redact as a reviewable diff, approved before anything leaves
```

# Candidate causal chains, and the 8D

---

## Part 1 — Ranked candidates, never a verdict

**A confident wrong root cause is worse than a ranked list, because it closes
the investigation.** Everyone stops looking, a corrective action gets
implemented against the wrong mechanism, it fails, and the next occurrence is a
recurrence after a closed CAPA — the most serious finding in the vocabulary.

So the output is always **ranked candidates with supporting and contradicting
evidence**, never one unqualified answer.

### State each candidate as a chain

Not a label. A chain of steps, each one carrying its own evidence:

> **Candidate 1 — material hardness above nominal**
> `LOT-77219 hardness 232 HB against 187–217 HB required` → `tool wear
> accelerated across the run` → `true position drifted out at OP30`
>
> **For:** material cert on the lot reports 232 HB (cert-77219.pdf p2). All 14
> out-of-tolerance parts trace to LOT-77219, none to LOT-77188 run on the same
> cell that week.
> **Against:** spindle load rose across the run on both lots, which a
> material-only cause does not explain.
> **What would confirm it:** hardness-test three retained parts from each lot.
> **What would kill it:** LOT-77188 parts showing the same drift on re-measure.

Chains matter because they are testable at each link, and because a link with no
evidence behind it is where the reasoning is actually weak. A one-word cause
hides that; a chain exposes it.

### Rank by evidential strength, and say what would settle it

Every candidate carries **the test that would confirm it and the test that would
kill it.** That is what turns a ranked list into a plan — the quality engineer
picks the cheapest discriminating test rather than working the list top-down.

**Where two candidates are supported equally, present both.** Do not break the
tie artificially to produce a cleaner-looking answer. A stated tie is a real
finding: it says the evidence on hand cannot separate them, and it names the
test that would.

### Symptom versus root cause

Keep pushing until the answer is something a system-level change could prevent.

| Symptom | Root cause underneath it |
|---|---|
| The operator misread the print | Two revisions were in circulation and the shop copy was uncontrolled |
| The tool was worn | The tool-change interval was set for a different material |
| The gage read wrong | Calibration lapsed and nothing flagged it |

The left column tells you who to talk to. The right column tells you what to
change so it cannot happen again — which is what D7 needs.

---

## Part 2 — The 8D

Eight disciplines. Many customers, especially in automotive and aerospace,
contractually require this format, which is precisely why it is a good drafting
target: **it is a fixed shape.**

| | Discipline | Drafted from |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Team | Names from the NCR — who found it, who owns quality — as a proposed team the owner edits |
| D2 | Problem description | The NCR: quantified what, where, when, how many, against which requirement |
| D3 | Interim containment | The NCR's containment plan, by location, with what has already been done |
| D4 | Root cause | The leading candidate **with its ranking and contradicting evidence intact** |
| D5 | Chosen corrective actions | Actions that address D4 specifically, each traceable to the link in the chain it breaks |
| D6 | Implement and verify | **Structured placeholder.** Needs a real-world outcome |
| D7 | Prevent recurrence | The system-level change so the class of problem cannot return |
| D8 | Close and recognize | **Structured placeholder.** Needs human sign-off |

### D6 and D8 stay empty on purpose

They require things that have not happened yet: proof that the action worked,
and a person signing their name. **Leave them as structured placeholders with
the fields laid out** — never pre-filled, never with plausible text a reviewer
might skim past and accept.

An 8D with a drafted D6 is a false record of verification, and in an audit it is
much worse than an incomplete one.

### D4 keeps its uncertainty

The temptation is to flatten the ranked candidates into a single confident D4
because that is what the form looks like it wants. Resist it.

Where the leading candidate is not clearly ahead, D4 says so and names the test
that would settle it. A customer reading an honest D4 with a stated confidence
and a verification plan is being told the truth about where the investigation
stands. That is what the discipline is for.

### D5 traces to D4, link by link

Each corrective action names **which link in the causal chain it breaks.** An
action that does not attach to a link is not a corrective action, it is an
improvement — worth doing, but it belongs somewhere else, and mixing the two is
how a CAPA closes without fixing anything.

### D7 is where recurrence gets prevented

D5 fixes this problem. D7 stops the class of problem. Incoming hardness
verification on that material, a controlled-print process, a calibration alarm
that actually fires — the change that means the mechanism cannot reach a part
again.

Where the recurrence check found a prior CAPA that failed, **D7 must address why
the earlier fix did not hold**, not simply restate it. Proposing the same action
that already failed once is the single most predictable way for this document to
be rejected.

## D2 — Problem description

- **What:** MB-1880 rev B, Bore A diameter oversize. The finding measured 22.034, 22.031 and 22.029 mm on 3 of 5 sampled parts. In-process rows for L-0412 measured 22.022 (seq 1), 22.029 (seq 90) and 22.034 (seq 180).

Already done, per the maintenance log: insert T7-0031 was replaced by T7-0032 at 2026-11-11 06:40. The first part after the change measured 22.007.

## D4 — Root cause (ranked candidates; not a single verdict)

**Confidence:** the evidence localises the cause to the T7 boring tool, but it cannot separate the two mechanisms below. **Tie for first place.**

1. **Insert T7-0031's edge changes progressively with parts cut** (edge build-up or chipping), and the bore grows.
   - For: 10 consecutive rising points on one insert; slope 0.000535 mm/h; R² 0.876; a 0.027 mm reset at the insert change; NCR-0219's cause.
   - Against: ordinary flank wear on a boring edge tends to cut undersize; no insert wear measurement exists.
2. **The boring head T7 setting creeps during the run**, and resets when the insert is changed and the head re-set.
   - For: the same trend and reset as candidate 1; the oversize direction fits a setting that opens up.
   - Weak point: no head-setting record exists at all.
3. **Coolant 6% → 8% (2026-11-08 16:00) contributes:** untested. There are 0 inspection rows before the change. L-0413 at 8% measured 22.007, which argues against coolant as the sole cause.
4. **Shift 2 practice:** weak. Shift and operator are fully confounded with time on the insert. Shift residuals are ±0.0012 mm (n = 5 each), and there are only 3 failures.

**Why it escaped (system-level root cause, from the evidence):**
- No in-process control on Bore A reacted to the drift. The trend rule was already firing within L-0409 to L-0411, and L-0411 seq 70 (22.019) was beyond the computed UCL of 22.0184 while still in spec.
- CAPA-071's interval is a part count, but parts cut per insert are not recorded anywhere in the inputs. Compliance cannot be shown: the insert had cut at least 211 parts at the first bad part and at least 510 by the end of L-0412, and both are floors.
- CAPA-071 was closed without verifying its effectiveness.

**Verification plan for D4** (the cheapest discriminating test):
- Read and record the T7 head setting on the presetter before the run on T7-0032 continues.
- Measure Bore A every ~50 parts for about the first 300 parts.
- Inspect removed insert T7-0031 for built-up edge or chipping.

A head setting that has not moved, with a bore that still rises, means candidate 1. A setting that moved means candidate 2. The same data, compared with any retained MB-1880 data from before 2026-11-08, tests candidate 3.

Owners and dates are left for the 8D owner. **The actions cover both tied candidates until the D4 test separates them**; afterwards, drop or keep A2 and A3 according to the result.

| A1 | **In-process Bore A check every 50 parts on VMC-03, with a reaction limit of 22.0176 mm.** Reaching it means: stop, change the insert, re-set the head. Until then, A1 governs. | Candidate 1, link "edge changes progressively with parts cut": the insert leaves service before its edge drives the bore out | | |

| A4 | **Parts-cut counter per insert ID** (insert ID and count recorded at each change and on each inspection row). | Candidate 1, link 1 ("insert in continuous service, count unknown"): makes the interval in A2 enforceable and auditable | | |

- **Not corrective actions (containment, in D3):** sorting and holding the 300, the L-0411 tail, and 100% inspection on T7-0032.
- **Improvement, not corrective action:** a standard offset/insert-change log at shift handover. It addresses the confounded shift-2 pattern, but that pattern is not supported as a cause.
- **Investigation, not corrective action:** the coolant comparison (D4 test). No coolant change is proposed, because no link supports one.

## D7 — Prevent recurrence (system level; addresses why CAPA-071 did not hold)

**Why CAPA-071 did not hold, from the evidence:**
- (a) Its 600-part interval was a fixed number set without a measured wear curve.
- (b) No record of parts cut per insert exists, so compliance could not be enforced or shown. This investigation could only establish floors.
- (c) It had no in-process detection: the drift was visible in data the plant already collected but did not chart.
- (d) It was closed with effectiveness "not verified" in April, and the same defect recurred in November.

Re-issuing a 600-part (or any fixed) interval would repeat (a) to (d), so it is not proposed.
